lessons.title: Light from sky and ground
body: A HemisphereLight gives surfaces a gradient between a sky color and a ground color based on their normal direction. It is a cheap way to suggest light coming from an environment.
It is not a full simulation of bounced light and does not cast shadows. Use it as a fill light, then let a directional or point light define stronger highlights and shadows.
lessons.hint: Change the intensity on the last line and watch the unlit side of the cube.

quiz.question: Does a HemisphereLight cast shadows?
quiz.explanation: HemisphereLight provides fill lighting without shadow maps.

lessons.title: A small sun for your scene
body: A DirectionalLight acts like a distant source: its rays are parallel and do not weaken with distance. Its direction runs from its position toward its target.

Move the key light to the other side and compare the cube’s faces. Changing its position changes the direction, not distance-based falloff. The default target is the origin; add a custom target to the scene if you move that target.
lessons.hint: The key light is named light. Change its final X assignment.

quiz.question: A directional light gets dimmer with distance…
quiz.explanation: Directional lights model parallel rays from a distant source.

lessons.title: Light from a single point
body: A PointLight shines in every direction from its position, like a small bulb. With the default physically based decay of 2, illumination falls off with the square of distance.

The tiny unlit sphere marks our bulb. Increase its intensity to reveal the nearby knot. Unlike a directional light, moving a point light closer changes both the lighting direction and the amount of light reaching the surface.
lessons.hint: Change the final intensity assignment. The marker itself stays bright because it is unlit.

quiz.question: A point light emits from…
quiz.explanation: Point lights model a small source emitting outward in all directions.

lessons.title: Anchor objects with shadows
body: A shadow makes an object feel connected to its surroundings. Shadow mapping renders depth from a light’s viewpoint, then compares surfaces against that depth.

Several switches must agree: renderer.shadowMap.enabled, light.castShadow, a mesh that casts, and a mesh that receives. The floor and light are ready. Enable the missing switch on the cube. Bigger shadow maps improve detail but consume more memory and drawing work.
lessons.hint: Set mesh.castShadow to true. The floor already has receiveShadow enabled.

quiz.question: Which surface usually needs receiveShadow?
quiz.explanation: A receiving surface is where the shadow should appear.

lessons.title: Give distance a color
body: Fog blends objects toward a color as their distance from the camera increases. It can give a small scene a strong sense of depth and hide a hard horizon.

THREE.Fog starts at near and reaches full fog at far. Those values are independent of the camera’s clipping planes. Matching the fog and background colors makes distant objects fade smoothly into the environment.
lessons.task: Set the fog’s far distance to 16.

quiz.question: Does fog remove distant geometry from the scene?
options: No, it changes its rendered color
Only if the fog is blue
quiz.explanation: Fog changes appearance. Clipping and culling determine what gets drawn.
